This results in a flat horizontal quad rather than a smoothly interpolated surface, as all four corners share this height [S1, unofficial].

The code calculates a single `height` value for each iteration of the inner loops (defined by `worldX` and `worldZ`). This same `height` value is then assigned to all six vertices of the two triangles (forming a quad) generated for that unit square. Specifically, the vertices are (worldX, height, worldZ), (worldX+1, height, worldZ), (worldX, height, worldZ+1), etc. Since all four corners of the resulting quad share the exact same `height` value, the resulting geometry is a flat horizontal plane (quad) rather than a surface interpolated between different heights at the corners.

Each quad corresponds to a unit square in the XZ plane [S1, unofficial].

The code iterates over a 2D grid (chunkX, chunkZ, x, z) to generate vertices. For each iteration, it calculates a height based on worldX and worldZ, then outputs two triangles that form a quad. The vertices of these quads are defined by (worldX, height, worldZ), (worldX+1, height, worldZ), etc. This structure confirms that each generated quad corresponds to a unit square in the XZ plane (spanning from worldX to worldX+1 and worldZ to worldZ+1), with the Y coordinate determined by the height function.
